question: to the Commission Cynthia Ní Mhurchú (Renew) Subject:

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are designed to operate in a complementary manner, ensuring coherence between carbon pricing for domestic production and imports. While the revision of CBAM is ongoing and the EU ETS is scheduled for further review on 15 July 2026, questions arise regarding the interaction between these instruments in practice. In particular, the existence of accumulated free allowances under the EU ETS in certain sectors may create differing capacities among market participants to absorb carbon-related costs. This could potentially lead to distortions of competition between operators that have historically benefited from free allocations and those that have not, including importers subject to CBAM obligations. Given that free allowances are intended to support the decarbonisation of energy-intensive industries, the accumulation of significant unused stocks also raises questions regarding their effective use and their impact on market dynamics. Against this background: 1.
How does the Commission assess the potential impact of accumulated free allowances on competition and the level playing field in sectors covered by the CBAM?
Does the Commission envisage measures, in the context of the upcoming reviews, to address possible imbalances arising from such situations?
How does the Commission ensure that free allowances under the EU ETS effectively contribute to the decarbonisation objectives in the sectors concerned?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The Commission’s proposal to revise the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) was adopted on 17 July 20261. It has a strong focus on clean investment, providing further support and incentives to industry, and establishing a predictable and pragmatic emissions reduction pathway to support the business case for investment in Europe. As part of this, it proposes to modernise free allocation by linking continued support beyond 2030 to investing in decarbonisation in the EU. As part of the proposal, free allocation will continue to be phased out gradually (by 2038) in step with the phase-in of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The Market Stability Reserve (MSR) is the main EU ETS tool for dealing with historical surplus of allowances. The proposal also modernises the MSR for the post-2030 period, building on a separate proposal presented by the Commission in April 20262. In keeping with previous assessments, the Commission focused on a predictable, rule-based forward approach and does not consider retroactive adjustments of private allowance holdings.
